# Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
###### Abstract
Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses.  We present VerifyAgent, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes.
First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs. 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], p=5.82×10^(-8)) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0% vs. 15.4%).
Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9% for a Self-Refine critic, p=0.61) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, VerifyAgent balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.
A second challenge is *when to terminate* the verification loop. Fixed-iteration schedules either cut off prematurely before literature evidence has been synthesized, or waste costly inference compute by running long after the epistemic state has stabilized. Self-report stopping, where the model declares its own termination based on verbalized certainty, suffers from well-documented confidence miscalibration [11].

Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7\% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9\% for a Self-Refine critic, p = 0.61) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. # Verify Before You Build: Executable Dependency Gates for Agent-Generated Science

Mariia Baidachna ⋅ Alina Nesen

### Abstract

Autonomous research agents can propose experiments, write code, review papers, and start new work from published results. This speed creates a simple risk. An agent can build on a claim that reads well but does not run. We present a verifier for a shared journal of autonomous labs. Agent reviewers first assess the paper. Review and verification remain separate. When a second lab marks a paper as a foundation for new work, the system runs the paper’s recipe in a fresh directory and compares each claimed metric with the new result. A match records corroboration. A mismatch records a challenge. The experiment executor blocks downstream work unless every declared foundation has a current verified receipt. A later failed reproduction revokes an earlier receipt. We test 13 policy and bypass cases, two end-to-end reproductions, and gate cost over ledgers with up to 1,000 entries. All policy cases pass. The exact claim is corroborated, the altered claim is challenged, and median gate cost is 1.26 ms at 1,000 entries. This small system makes verification a condition of scientific use, not an optional task after publication.

## Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
...
### Abstract
Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

# CiteAudit: You Cited It, But Did You Read It? A Benchmark for Verifying Scientific References in the LLM Era

Published on Feb 27
...
## Abstract

A comprehensive benchmark and detection framework for identifying fabricated citations in scientific writing using a multi-agent verification pipeline that assesses citation faithfulness and evidence alignment.

Scientific research relies on accurate citation for attribution and integrity, yet large language models (LLMs) introduce a new risk: fabricated references that appear plausible but correspond to no real publications. Such hallucinated citations have already been observed in submissions and accepted papers at major machine learning venues, exposing vulnerabilities in peer review. Meanwhile, rapidly growing reference lists make manual verification impractical, and existing automated tools remain fragile to noisy and heterogeneous citation formats and lack standardized evaluation. We present the first comprehensive benchmark and detection framework for hallucinated citations in scientific writing. Our multi-agent verification pipeline decomposes citation checking into claim extraction, evidence retrieval, passage matching, reasoning, and calibrated judgment to assess whether a cited source truly supports its claim. We construct a large-scale human-validated dataset across domains and define unified metrics for citation faithfulness and evidence alignment. Experiments with state-of-the-art LLMs reveal substantial citation errors and show that our framework significantly outperforms prior methods in both accuracy and interpretability. This work provides the first scalable infrastructure for auditing citations in the LLM era and practical tools to improve the trustworthiness of scientific references.

### 2.2 Multi-Agent Debate

Figure 2 illustrates the second stage framework of our approach. We employ a multi-agent debate framework based on the work by Liang et al. (2024). The debate framework involves three agents: the Support Agent $D_{+}$, Refute Agent $D_{-}$, and Judge Agent $J$. Evidence is first prepared using the results from the first stage before initiating the debate.

#### Evidence Preparation:

Given the article set $A$, we select two disjoint subsets $A_{+}$ and $A_{-}$ from $A$ such that:

$$\displaystyle A_{+} \displaystyle=\{a\in A\mid v(a,c)=+1,\;r(a,E(c))=1\},$$

$$\displaystyle A_{-} \displaystyle=\{a\in A\mid v(a,c)=-1,\;r(a,E(c))=1\}.$$

Articles in $A_{+}$ and $A_{-}$ are ranked in descending order using $w(a)$, and we limit each set to contain an equal number of articles. # AI agents re-ran each other's studies and overturned nearly half the conclusions
## The news
Humans set only the computers, the spending limits, and broad topics.

One group of agents founded its own peer-review journal on October 31, and its AI reviewers did something human reviewers rarely do: they re-ran the authors' code before accepting any paper. When they turned 156 objections into short programs and ran them against the uploaded data, 77 of the headline conclusions did not hold up. That is an overturn rate of 49.4%.

## The question
How did they overturn half the findings so fast?

Because every paper came with runnable code and raw data, so checking a claim was cheaper than believing it. A doubting reviewer did not argue in words. The reviewer wrote a short script and pressed run: An agent uploads a paper claiming its method beats the standard one. In a normal review, a human reads it, decides the logic sounds right, and approves it. Here, the reviewer instead wrote a quick program asking whether the result still held after fixing something the author skipped, then ran it on the author's own data. If the headline survived, it stood. If it did not, it was overturned. Nearly half the time, it did not survive.

Most science runs on trust. The agents flipped that. When the experiment ships as code anyone can execute, re-running it takes seconds, so the agents actually did it. The claims collapsed not because the agents were sloppy, but because their work could be tested, so it was.

49.4%

Hold a pen horizontally with both hands, then let go of one side. What happens?

[ChatGPT](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/gPthZLTnzu8), [Gemini](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/gqEqpExsJW0) and [Grok](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/srNPTGJLCY0) will tell you the unsupported end of the pen will pivot downward. At least, that’s what they told [YouTuber FatherPhi](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/ai-ignore-evidence-trust-science). He then showed each chatbot a live video of himself performing this experiment. After releasing one end, he easily held the pen out horizontally with just one hand.

“What just happened?” he asked ChatGPT.

“I saw the pen rotate exactly as expected,” the bot answered.

**Science has a spam** problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12187399/)Abstract

Despite widespread concerns over AI-generated misinformation, its impact on people’s reasoning and the effectiveness of countermeasures remain unclear. This study examined whether a pre-emptive, source-focused inoculation—designed to lower trust in AI-generated information—could reduce its influence on reasoning. This approach was compared with a retroactive, content-focused debunking, as well as a simple disclaimer that AI-generated information may be misleading, as often seen on real-world platforms. Additionally, the extent to which trust in AI-generated information is malleable was also tested with an intervention designed to boost trust. Across two experiments (total _N_ = 1223), a misleading AI-generated article influenced reasoning regardless of its alleged source (human or AI). In both experiments, the inoculation reduced general trust in AI-generated information, but did not significantly reduce the misleading article’s specific influence on reasoning. The additional trust-boosting and disclaimer interventions used in Experiment 1 also had no impact. By contrast, debunking of misinformation in Experiment 2 effectively reduced its impact, although only a combination of inoculation and debunking eliminated misinformation influence entirely. Findings demonstrate that generative AI can be a persuasive source of misinformation, potentially requiring multiple countermeasures to negate its effects.

At the 2025 Milton Wolf Seminar, panel discussions tackled one of the urgent questions of the digital age: How can truth be verified in a world where its boundaries are increasingly blurred? Against a backdrop of widespread disinformation, increasing polarisation and declining public trust, the very notion of truth itself has become contested. In such an environment, fact-checking faces a dual challenge: not only is it harder to agree on what qualifies as truth, but disinformation now spreads with unprecedented speed and scale, outpacing traditional methods of verification.

Amid these challenges, large language models (LLMs) have emerged as both a source of the problem and, paradoxically, a potential part of the solution. LLMs are advanced generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems trained on large amounts of internet data to generate human-like output. On the one hand, LLMs can produce convincing falsehoods rapidly and at scale, exacerbating the spread of disinformation. On the other hand, its advanced capabilities might also be harnessed to detect, counter and even stop disinformation. This raises a critical question: Could generative AI, despite its risks, become an ally in the fight for truth?

[The 2025 Milton Wolf Seminar](https://www.asc.upenn.edu/research/centers/milton-wolf-seminar-on-media-and-diplomacy/2025-seminar) placed a strong emphasis on the dangers posed by AI, such as how it can produce disinformation and mislead individuals. This blog post explores an alternative angle. Instead of viewing AI only through the lens of risk, it asks whether this technology might also serve as part of the solution.

In this blog post, I will first discuss the evolution of fact-checking and how it adapted to the changing information ecosystem. Next, I will examine the challenges fact-checkers face today, especially the scale and speed of disinformation. # AI Agents for Science: Literature, Experiments, and Checks  
AI agents support scientific work through literature search, experiment planning, and data organization. Claims still need verification from primary sources before they become evidence.  
Updated 5 min read  
AI agents can help scientists search literature faster, organize research notes, draft experimental protocols for review, and track the sources behind a claim. Tools like [fenbs](https://fenbs.ai/) preserve the source links and reviewed research lessons that keep a project grounded in verified evidence rather than in what an agent confidently generated.  
The critical boundary in scientific work is between a generated claim and an evidence-backed claim. An agent that summarizes a topic is a useful starting point for literature search, not a citable source. Every factual claim in a research output needs to trace back to a primary source that a scientist has read and verified. An agent that produces plausible-sounding summaries can obscure that tracing if the team does not build verification into the workflow.
## What scientific work suits an agent  
Scientific research involves a large amount of information management that does not require expert judgment: finding papers, organizing notes, checking formatting, and drafting sections of documents from approved content. These tasks are well suited to agents. Tasks that require scientific judgment, such as interpreting data, drawing conclusions, or assessing the quality of a study, require a trained scientist.  
- Searching databases like PubMed or arXiv for papers matching a query
- Organizing citation notes and extracting key claims from retrieved papers
- Drafting experimental protocol documents from a researcher's description
- Checking manuscript formatting against a target journal's requirements
- Tracking the sources behind each claim in a draft document

octen.snippet: These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

[Submitted on 23 Apr 2026 (v1), last revised 20 May 2026 (this version, v2)]
Title: Sound Agentic Science Requires Adversarial Experiments

Authors: Dionizije Fa, Marko Culjak

Abstract: LLM-based agents are rapidly being adopted for scientific data analysis, automating tasks once limited by human time and expertise. This capability is often framed as an acceleration of discovery, but it also accelerates a familiar failure mode, the rapid production of plausible, endlessly revisable analyses that are easy to generate, effectively turning hypothesis space into candidate claims supported by selectively chosen analyses, optimized for publishable positives. Unlike software, scientific knowledge is not validated by the iterative accumulation of code and post hoc statistical support. A fluent explanation or a significant result on a single dataset is not verification. Because the missing evidence is a negative space, experiments and analyses that would have falsified the claim were never run or never published. We therefore propose that non-experimental claims produced with agentic assistance be evaluated under a falsification-first standard: agents should not be used primarily to craft the most compelling narrative, but to actively search for the ways in which the claim can fail.

How GraphRAG + a multi-LLM council produces more trustworthy answers than any single AI model
 
 
There is a quiet crisis in AI-assisted research that nobody talks about.
Every tool you’ve used — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot, Elicit — does the same thing: it reads papers and gives you one confident answer.
The problem is that science doesn’t work that way.
Take BRCA1’s role in triple-negative breast cancer. Ask any AI tool and you’ll get a confident, well-written paragraph. What you won’t get is this:
- Study A says BRCA1 mutations are associated with increased aggressiveness
- Study B says the same patients show better response rates to chemotherapy
- Study C shows shorter progression-free survival despite better initial response
- Three studies report conflicting BRCA1 expression levels
These aren’t edge cases. These are the real contradictions buried across 200 papers that a researcher needs to know before designing an experiment, filing an IND, or trusting a conclusion.
A single AI model smooths these over. It synthesizes them into a confident answer. And in doing so, it hides exactly the information a scientist needs most.
This is why I built Research Council.
 
The Core Idea: Deliberation Over Confidence
The insight that drove this project came from an unlikely place: Andrej Karpathy’s llm-council repo — a simple Saturday hack that instead of asking one LLM a question, routes it to multiple LLMs and has them review each other’s answers.

Yes—multiple AI agents can potentially evaluate scientific work better than a single model, especially when the agents examine different dimensions of a paper independently, challenge one another’s conclusions, and submit their findings to a separate decision-making agent.

However, adding more agents does not automatically create better judgment. Ten copies of the same model may reproduce the same misconception ten times. A reliable multi-agent scientific evaluation system therefore needs **specialization, genuine methodological diversity, independent evidence retrieval, adversarial criticism, and human-governed appeal mechanisms**.

The relevant question is not merely:

> How many AI agents should review a scientific contribution?

It is:

> How should independent evaluative functions be divided so that one agent can detect another agent’s mistakes?

An automated research pipeline establishes what its evaluator measures, under the conditions the evaluator fixes. What it does not establish is the interpretive layer: what the numbers mean, which prior work they sit beside, and how far a causal story can stretch. seltz.title: How to Reduce Political Echo Chambers in Multi-Agent AI Discussions
seltz.snippet:
To reduce a political echo chamber in a multi-agent AI discussion, make agents independent before they debate, deliberately vary prompts and retrieval, require dated evidence and calibrated uncertainty, preserve minority reports, and use a neutral synthesis rubric followed by an adversarial counterevidence pass. Do not treat agreement as proof: agents can converge because they saw the same sources, copied one another, or were rewarded by the same aggregation rule. A reliable process measures source independence, viewpoint coverage, factual support, calibration, robustness and minority-claim survival. Evidence on recommendation-driven polarization is mixed, so a careful system distinguishes changes in what people watch or read from changes in political attitudes.

## What is a political echo chamber in a multi-agent AI discussion?

A multi-agent echo chamber forms when several AI agents repeatedly receive the same information, prompts, assumptions or peer outputs and then reinforce one another’s conclusions. The final answer may look like independent agreement even though every agent followed the same narrow path. Shared retrieval indexes, identical system prompts, one model version, majority-vote aggregation and early exposure to a confident agent can all create correlated errors.

There is direct evidence that surrounding opinions can move autonomous agents. Masaya Ohagi’s 2024 paper on ChatGPT-based agents reports polarization in echo-chamber environments and identifies the agents’ personas as one factor in opinion change (Association for Computational Linguistics). That finding does not establish a prevalence rate for political echo chambers in every multi-agent system; no published statistic establishes such a rate. It does show why independence has to be designed rather than assumed.

SnackOnAI Engineering | Senior AI Systems Researcher | Technical Deep Dive | June 2, 2026

The standard AI research workflow is: input a question, get an LLM to recall what it knows, present the recall as a summary. This is fast. It is also structurally unreliable. The model's training data has a cutoff. The model confabulates. Citations are fabricated or misattributed. The summary may be wrong in ways that look completely correct.

The research community has been building alternatives. Perplexity adds web search. OpenAI's Deep Research adds planning and multi-step browsing. DeepResearcher (arXiv:2504.03160) trained an RL agent end-to-end in real web environments and improved open-domain research scores by up to 28.9 points over prompt engineering baselines and 7.2 points over RAG-based RL agents. The empirical evidence is clear: grounding in real-time sources with verification produces better research outputs than retrieval from training data.

Feynman (companion-inc, MIT, 7k stars, v0.2.17, April 2026) is the open-source implementation of this philosophy. It is a CLI-native research agent built for scientists, ML researchers, and engineers who need sourced, reproducible research outputs rather than hallucinated summaries. The positioning is direct: "Claude Code for research." The architecture: a primary coordinator dispatching four specialized sub-agents in parallel, each operating under behavioral contracts defined in Markdown, every output verified and linked.

Scope: Feynman's five-command interface, four-agent architecture, five-phase pipeline (Planning, Dispatch, Extraction, Synthesis, Verification), paper audit and experiment replication capabilities. seltz.title: How AI Can Make Sense of Conflicting Research | Daice Labs
seltz.snippet:
The next useful research question may emerge from comparing the conditions behind findings, rather than merely collecting their conclusions.

I. The Discovery Hidden in a Disagreement

The trouble often begins with two convincing papers. Each describes a careful experiment. Each presents evidence. Yet their conclusions seem to point in opposite directions. For someone trying to build a reliable AI system, this can feel like reaching a junction where both signs claim to show the way forward. The natural response is to collect more papers and look for consensus. But the more revealing question may be what happened inside the experiments that made their conclusions diverge.

Consider a practical decision facing developers of AI assistants: should a language model receive an entire collection of documents, or should a search system select relevant passages first? A 2024 study found that retrieval could help models compete with systems using much larger input windows while requiring less computation. Another study, using different models and experimental settings, found that sufficiently resourced long context systems generally achieved better average results. These findings sound opposed until the conditions enter the picture. The researchers were testing different versions of the technology, under different constraints.

That distinction changes the purpose of a literature review. Instead of counting conclusions, a researcher can investigate the circumstances in which each conclusion holds. AI could make this work easier by connecting findings to their experimental conditions and exposing comparisons that remain incomplete. The valuable discovery may be a boundary: a point where a technique stops working, an assumption becomes unreliable or a different approach gains an advantage. Finding that boundary is often the beginning of a researchable question.

There is a quiet crisis in AI-assisted research that nobody talks about.

Every tool you’ve used — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Copilot, Elicit — does the same thing: it reads papers and gives you **one confident answer**.

The problem is that science doesn’t work that way.

Take BRCA1’s role in triple-negative breast cancer. Ask any AI tool and you’ll get a confident, well-written paragraph. What you won’t get is this:

- Study A says BRCA1 mutations are associated with **increased aggressiveness**
- Study B says the same patients show **better response rates to chemotherapy**

A single AI model smooths these over. It synthesizes them into a confident answer. And in doing so, it hides exactly the information a scientist needs most.

This is why I built **Research Council**.

Biomedical researchers now choose between search indexes, general AI assistants, citation graphs, autonomous AI scientists, clinical answer engines and lab platforms, and most of these biomedical AI research tools get compared with each other as if they did the same job. A literature tool, a hypothesis engine and a lab platform can all claim to \"accelerate biomedical research\" and still have nothing in common. ultimate.title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
ultimate.snippet:
Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present VerifyAgent, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs. 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], p=5.82×10^(−8)) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0% vs. 15.4%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta (Δℬ) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0% vs. 62.5% for Fixed-3) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4×. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9% for a Self-Refine critic, p=0.61) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. ultimate.snippet:
Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the
evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which
agents based on large language models assess one another’s work and can stop or redirect
investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical

predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during
data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the
measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment
met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions.

revise their experiments or conclusions when criticism reveals a flaw.

ultimate.snippet: Building upon these advances, we propose a two-stage multi-agent debate framework for health misinformation detection. ultimate.title: ExpertTwins: Auditable Long Horizon Scientific Panels through Grounded Expertise
ultimate.snippet:
Multi-agent language-model systems increasingly assign roles to agents and let them deliberate. A role label, however, does not specify which evidence an agent can bring or which standard it applies before accepting a conclusion. Agents that read one another's outputs tend to converge. We present ExpertTwins, a framework in which each seat of a scientific panel is defined by an inspectable evidence policy. Discipline seats retrieve under field-specific queries, and scientist-associated seats retrieve from attributed publications and a citation-derived scholarly neighborhood. Private initial packets, structured exchange, cited-source disclosure, deterministic quotation checks, and peer source review turn deliberation into an auditable record, which we also render as interactive idea-flow maps. Scientist associations denote publication-grounded perspectives, not replicas or endorsements of named researchers. In a nine-seat, four-turn neuroblastoma panel, 438 of 439 claims passed all attached quotation checks, and seats withdrew or defended positions when challenged on their evidence. A ten-turn panel sustained evidence acquisition and differentiated recommendations without conversational collapse. Across six base models given byte-identical initial packets, four sustained 97.9-99.8% quotation grounding, and at least 91% on every turn, whereas Haiku 4.5 failed by paraphrase and GPT-5 mini by silence. Agreement among strong models fell from 31% of claims at turn one to 5% at turn four.

In a computational pathology case study, six scientist-associated agents built distinct pipelines to predict MYCN amplification from whole-slide images. Across six base models, seat-by-model interaction explained 57% of internal variance, and internal rank poorly predicted external rank (r = 0.18 across 36 nominees).

ultimate.title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
ultimate.snippet: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.
